newsitem.title: UK: Eurobonds see jumbo mark and lira deals.
newsitem.headline: Eurobonds see jumbo mark and lira deals.

text.p: The Eurobond market's main deals on Thursday were two 1.0 billion mark seven-year bonds.

RHEINHYP issued a 1.0 billion mark seven-year Pfandbrief, German domestic mortgage-backed bonds, which had three non-German underwriters in an effort to place the paper outside Germany. RHEINHYP has already worked on expanding it investor base when it launched a dollar-denominated Pfandbrief in May.
Thursday's deal was priced to offer one basis point over Bunds, and bankers said this was not much inducement to foreign investors to buy the Pfandbrief instead of Bunds.
In terms of domestic Pfanbrief levels, the pricing was in line, they said.
"RHEINHYP was very well-accepted, but only domestically," a Frankfurt-based syndicate manager said.
"For international accounts it is difficult to sell at current levels. All recent jumbos have only been placed with domestic customers because there is not enough of a pick-up over Bunds," he said.

But a syndicate manager at BZW, joint lead manager of the deal, said they had marketed Pfandbrief bonds to British institutions over the last weeks and had sold over 100 million marks of the bond to these accounts.
"Relative to Libor it looks quite attractive, and the underlying Bund trades way above par," the BZW official said. "There is a lot of demand for this product in the UK."
The other lead managers of the deal were ABN AMRO Hoare Govett, CDC Marche, Dresdner Kleinwort Benson and HSBC Trinkaus.

DSL Finance launched a straight 1.0 billion mark seven-year Eurobond at five notches over Bunds. Dealers said the paper would be placed in Europe over time, but was not immediately appealing to investors.
"There are Deutsche Ausgleichsbank and Dresdner 2004 deals outstanding, and these are three to four b.p. cheaper than DSL," a Euromark trader said.
Late in the morning the World Bank launched a 1.0 trillion lire January 2007 bond, which paid a 9.3 percent coupon until January 2, 1999, the day EMU is due to start.
The coupon then becomes 5.4 percent. The deal comes after a flood of lira bonds, demand for which has boomed on the back of increased expectations that Italy will join EMU in 1999.
The spread between Italian BTPs and German Bunds was at 96 b.p. on Thursday. A month ago it stood at around 150 b.p.
On the emerging markets side reports that Lebanon was considering a $1.0 billion 30-year bond issue surprised emerging market analysts.
They said it was unlikely there would be any demand for such a maturity due to the political uncertainty in Lebanon, although it could possibly raise such an amount at a shorter maturity.
